analysis.one_liner: Guarantees emergency paid sick leave, free coronavirus testing, and expanded food and unemployment aid during the COVID-19 crisis.
analysis.headline: The bill became law just a week after introduction, passing the House 363-40 and the Senate 90-8, guaranteeing paid sick leave, free COVID-19 testing, and emergency food and unemployment aid.
analysis.plain_summary: This law, written and passed in about a week as COVID-19 shut the country down, required most employers to give workers paid sick leave and paid family leave, required insurers and government health programs to cover coronavirus testing at no cost, and expanded food and unemployment assistance. It sent federal money to states, schools, and food banks to keep families fed during school closures, and it fully reimbursed employers for the leave wages they pay through tax credits. The paid leave provisions were temporary, expiring at the end of 2020.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who get sick, are quarantined, or lose child care at employers with fewer than 500 employees get paid time off. Families get free COVID-19 testing with no copay or deductible under nearly every form of coverage, including an option for the uninsured. Low-income households get bigger SNAP food benefits, suspended work requirements, and replacement benefits for school meals their children miss. States get extra federal Medicaid money and $1 billion in unemployment administration grants. Self-employed workers get refundable tax credits to cover their own sick leave.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers, families, and the unemployed

how_it_helps.text: Gives full-time workers 80 hours of paid sick leave, at up to $511 per day, if they are sick with COVID-19, under a quarantine order, advised to self-quarantine, or caring for someone who is, available immediately with no minimum time on the job.

Gives parents up to 12 weeks of leave at two-thirds pay, capped at $200 per day and $10,000 total, when a school or child care provider closes for COVID-19, with job protection and a right to an equivalent position.

Requires private insurance, Medicare, Medicare Advantage, Medicaid, CHIP, VA, TRICARE, and the Indian Health Service to cover COVID-19 testing and related visits with no copays, deductibles, or prior authorization, and lets state Medicaid programs cover testing for uninsured people at 100% federal cost.

Suspends SNAP work requirements, lets states give households the maximum monthly food benefit as an emergency allotment, and lets states pay families the value of school meals their children miss during closures — the program that became known as pandemic EBT.

Puts $1 billion into state unemployment offices to process a flood of claims, covers 100% of the federal share of extended unemployment benefits through the end of 2020, and encourages states to waive work-search rules and the waiting week.

Increases the federal government's share of Medicaid costs for every state and territory during the emergency, on the condition that states do not tighten eligibility rules beyond what was in effect on January 1, 2020.
Funds WIC ($500 million), food banks ($400 million), and home-delivered meals for seniors ($250 million), and lets WIC clients recertify without visiting a clinic in person.

analysis.who_pays: The federal Treasury pays the emergency appropriations and reimburses employers for the leave wages they front through tax credits funded by transfers from the general fund; Social Security trust funds are made whole for the payroll taxes not collected on leave wages. Private insurers and self-insured plans bear the cost of covering testing and related visits at no charge during the emergency. Employers with fewer than 500 employees must pay leave wages upfront, though the tax credits give them 100% back, and larger employers are exempt from the mandate altogether.

drawbacks.text: The paid leave mandates apply only to employers with fewer than 500 employees, so workers at large corporations get nothing from this law, and employers of health care workers and emergency responders — many of them the people most exposed to the virus — can opt out of covering their own staff.

Businesses with fewer than 50 employees can be exempted from the leave requirements if compliance would threaten the business's survival, and the Labor Department can also exclude health providers and emergency responders.
Family leave is far weaker than sick leave: the first 10 days are unpaid unless the worker spends their own accrued leave, and after that it pays only two-thirds of wages, capped at $200 a day.

The version of the bill that became law dropped a provision from the introduced bill that would have required OSHA to issue an emergency standard forcing employers to protect health care workers from infection on the job.

The law gives manufacturers, distributors, and users of respiratory protective devices, such as N95 masks, liability protection for their use from January 2020 through October 2024, shielding a specific industry from suits while workers depended on that equipment.
All of the leave provisions expire on December 31, 2020, even if the pandemic and its economic damage continued past that date.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For workers and families facing a sudden national shutdown, the benefits were large and immediate: paid time off to be sick or to care for children, free testing, and food money arriving through existing programs. The costs — emergency federal spending and temporary insurer obligations — were modest by the standards of the crisis response. The honest criticisms are about design, not size: the law skips workers at companies with 500 or more employees, lets hospitals and first-responder employers opt out of covering their own people, dropped the workplace-safety standard for health care workers that was in the original bill, and pairs genuine help for workers with a liability shield for mask manufacturers. It was a first emergency package, patched quickly, and the weakest workers at the largest employers were the ones left out.

outcome.mechanism: Passed by wide bipartisan votes in both chambers in the same week it was introduced and signed by the president the day the Senate passed it.

narrative.text: The bill was introduced on March 11, 2020, as the pandemic closed schools and workplaces across the country.
Three days later the House passed it 363-40 under a fast-track procedure requiring a two-thirds vote; every House Democrat who voted was in favor, while 40 Republicans voted no.
The Senate passed it 90-8 without amendment on March 18; all 8 no votes came from Republicans.
The president signed it the same day it passed the Senate, making it Public Law 116-127.
Between introduction and passage, the OSHA emergency temporary standard to protect health care workers from infection — included in the original bill — was dropped from the version that became law.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Working people who needed paid leave, free testing, and food aid gained directly, and they got it fast. Employers came out ahead too, since the government reimburses their leave costs in full, and respirator makers gained a four-year liability shield. The workplace-safety rule for health care workers was the main thing that did not survive.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers who used the leave; employers reimbursed in full

sides.party_line_note: The bill passed with overwhelming support from both parties: every voting House Democrat and every Senate Democrat voted yes, and 140 of 197 House Republicans and 43 of 53 Senate Republicans joined them, with all 48 no votes coming from Republicans.

industries.note: They must front paid sick and family leave wages for their workers, but the law reimburses them 100% through payroll tax credits, and firms under 50 employees can get a hardship exemption. The mandate is real but the out-of-pocket cost is largely covered.

They must cover COVID-19 testing, administration, and related visits with no cost sharing and no prior authorization for the duration of the emergency, absorbing claims they would otherwise have billed to patients.

The law gives makers, distributors, and users of covered respiratory protective devices liability protection from January 2020 through October 2024, reducing their litigation exposure while the public relied on their equipment.
Emergency SNAP allotments at the maximum monthly benefit and replacement benefits for missed school meals pushed federal food money through stores during the shutdown.
Free testing brought more people in the door without cost barriers, but the law lets these employers exclude their own health care workers and emergency responders from the paid leave guarantees.
